set.overview: The standard way up Redcloud is a Class 2 walk on a maintained trail, finishing along a broad ridge to the 14,000-foot summit in the San Juan Mountains near Lake City. It follows Silver Creek into a high basin, gains a saddle near 13,000 feet, and turns west along the northeast ridge, where a false summit sits below the real top. There is no technical climbing, only rocky tread near the summit.
set.approach: Start at the Silver Creek and Grizzly Gulch trailhead, about 10,400 feet on County Road 30 toward Cinnamon Pass; it is roughly 2 miles south of Lake City on Colorado 149, then nearly 16 miles of dirt road with a shelf section along the south side of Sunshine Peak. The trail heads northeast through forest and beside Silver Creek, then bends southeast near 12,000 feet into the basin below the peak, about 3 miles and 2,000 feet in. From there it climbs south toward the saddle between a 13,561-foot point and Redcloud, where you turn west onto the northeast ridge.
set.descent_text: Retrace the ascent route: back along the northeast ridge to the 13,000-foot saddle, then down the trail into the basin and along Silver Creek to the trailhead. It is an out-and-back, with no separate descent line.
hazards: Snow often lingers in the basin below the peak into early summer
A false summit near 13,900 feet and a faint trail on the upper ridge make the top easy to misjudge
Loose rock on the Class 2 ground near the summit
Rough, narrow shelf road on the drive in, which can need clearance in some years

evidence.fact: 9 miles round trip, so 4.5 miles one way (7.24 km)

review.notes: Distance single-source: another page lists 4.5 miles out-and-back, ambiguous whether one way, so not counted as agreement. A second page states the summit is about 4.5 miles from the trailhead but cites the same publisher family. Season Jul-Aug is the window a conservation group's page recommends after snowmelt. Descent is a retrace of an out-and-back; no page describes a separate descent.

set.overview: San Luis Peak is a Class 1 walk to the highest summit in the La Garita Wilderness, reached by a long trail up Stewart Creek. The route passes beaver ponds, breaks out of the trees near 12,000 feet, and climbs to a saddle before following the northeast ridge to the top. It is a remote, big-mileage day with gentle gradients and no scrambling.
set.approach: Drive dirt Forest Road 794 to the Stewart Creek trailhead at about 10,500 feet. A vehicle with good clearance is needed because the road crosses Pauline and Nutras Creeks on cement slabs. The trail follows Stewart Creek through forest past the upper creek and beaver ponds to treeline near 12,000 feet, then heads southwest into the upper basin, crosses the creek near 12,300 feet, and switchbacks to the 13,100-foot saddle. From the saddle the route traverses to the northeast ridge near 13,750 feet, crosses to its west side, and returns to the crest.
hazards: The trail near 3 miles can be hard to follow in spring or after recent treefall
Remote approach road with two creek crossings on concrete slabs needs a vehicle with clearance
Wilderness rules on party size, camping, fires and dogs apply from the boundary

evidence.fact: 13.5 miles round trip, so 6.75 miles one way (10.86 km)

review.notes: Single source for everything. Season and descent skipped: the page gives neither.

set.overview: Wetterhorn's southeast ridge is a Class 3 scramble to a 14,021-foot summit in the Uncompahgre Wilderness. After a saddle near 13,100 feet, the ridge passes a fin-like tower called the Prow, goes through the obvious notch above it, and finishes up the southwest face. The last 400 feet are on narrow sandy ledges that sometimes hold ice, and the exposure there is high.
set.approach: Drive Henson Creek Road (part of the Alpine Loop) about 11 miles from Lake City to the Matterhorn Creek junction. Vehicles without four-wheel drive park there and walk 0.7 mile to the Matterhorn Creek trailhead at roughly 10,800 feet; a high-clearance vehicle can drive the rest. From the upper trailhead the trail heads north, then branches onto the Wetterhorn trail near 12,000 feet and crosses rocky ground to the 13,100-foot saddle on the southeast ridge, where the scrambling begins.
hazards: High exposure on the upper ridge and the final ledges
Loose rock in places, though most ledges are solid
Sandy ledges on the last 400 feet can hold ice
Route-finding through the notch and past the Prow needs care

review.notes: Single source. Season and descent skipped: the page gives neither.

set.overview: Huron's standard trail is a Class 2 hike: forest switchbacks to timberline near 11,900 feet, a big grassy basin, and the saddle toward Browns Peak, then the rocky northern crest to the summit. The trail zigzags up to the north ridge crest at 13,500 feet and works onto the upper northwest face before regaining the ridge. The steepest, most eroded stretch lies between about 13,700 and 13,900 feet.
set.approach: From Buena Vista, drive about 14.5 miles north on U.S. 24 and turn left onto County Road 390, or turn right from Leadville after 20 miles south. Follow the dirt road about 12 miles to Winfield. A 2WD trailhead sits just past Winfield, while the Lake Ann trailhead, around 10,575 feet, is 2.1 miles farther on a rough 4WD road. The trail enters forest, crosses a stream, and switchbacks to treeline near 11,900 feet, then crosses a high basin to about 12,700 feet below the upper slopes.
hazards: Eroded trail with several parallel treads on the steep section around 13,700 to 13,900 feet
Loose rock on the upper slopes
The basin below treeline can be soggy in early summer
The 4WD road to the upper Lake Ann trailhead needs good clearance

review.notes: Single source. Season and descent skipped: the page gives neither.

set.overview: Sunshine Peak is climbed from the Silver Creek trailhead by first going over Redcloud Peak, then following the connecting ridge south. The Class 2 route climbs Redcloud's northeast ridge, crosses to the saddle near 13,500 feet, and climbs about 500 feet more to Sunshine's 14,004-foot top. The return passes back over Redcloud, adding a few hundred feet of regained climbing.
set.approach: Start at the Silver Creek and Grizzly Gulch trailhead near 10,400 feet on County Road 30, reached from Colorado 149 south of Lake City by about 16 miles of mostly dirt Alpine Loop road with a narrow shelf section. Follow the Silver Creek Trail northeast through forest to the basin near 12,000 feet, switchback to the 13,000-foot saddle, and climb Redcloud's northeast ridge to its summit about 4.5 miles in. From there a trail leads south along the ridge to the saddle and up to Sunshine.
set.descent_text: Return north along the ridge to Redcloud, regaining about 500 feet to its summit, then follow the ascent trail down to the basin and trailhead. Do not drop west from the Redcloud-Sunshine saddle: that gully is steep, loose and very hard to climb back out of.
hazards: The steep loose gully west of the Redcloud-Sunshine saddle, which is a poor shortcut off the ridge
Few bail-out options once you leave Redcloud's summit
Afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter on the exposed ridge
Cornices on the ridge and lingering snow in the basin early in the season

evidence.fact: 12.25 miles round trip, so 6.125 miles one way (9.86 km)

review.notes: Gain disputed: 4,800 vs 4,240 on a state trails page whose 5.8 mile distance looks inconsistent, so not locked. The route is by definition over Redcloud, so the figures include it; one-way is half the round trip, which includes re-climbing Redcloud on return (the 12.25 round trip is for the combined route). Season Jul-Aug is a conservation group's recommended window.

hazards: Exposed Fresh Air Traverse on the 5.7 section
Severe rope drag on the meandering line
Changing weather and strenuous climbing above 14,000 feet
Snow and ice can linger in the Mountaineers Route descent gully after storms

review.notes: Gain and distance skipped: no page found with East Face figures; the Mountaineers Route figure is a different line. The snow/ice descent hazard comes from an account of the neighbouring East Buttress, whose descent is the same gully, and matches the existing descent text.

set.overview: Williamson's West Face is the standard way up the mountain, a Class 3 route that starts from the Williamson Bowl, the glacier-carved basin below the peak, reached over Shepherd Pass. It runs up scree below a large black-streaked band of rock and up a wide chute, then follows a narrow cleft to the summit plateau. The cleft or chimney is the crux, and opinions on its difficulty vary from easy Class 3 to something harder, so a rope is sensible for beginners.
set.approach: Start at the Shepherd Pass trailhead west of Independence, reached on unpaved roads from Market Street and Foothill Road. The trail climbs past Anvil Camp, the main forested campsite, about 7 to 8 miles and 4,000 feet up, then roughly 2 more miles and 1,700 feet to Shepherd Pass, with a lake near the top for water. From the pass, go southeast into Williamson Bowl, follow cairns along the spine between the lakes, and head for the scree below the large black stain; camping in the bowl itself is discouraged.
set.descent_text: Come down the way you went up: the chute, the scree below the black stain, and the cleft or chimney, which needs careful downclimbing. Then recross Williamson Bowl and climb out to Shepherd Pass. The long slog out of the bowl at the end of the day is tiring, and the scree is easier going down than up.
hazards: Loose scree and sliding rock in the chute and on the crossing above the black stain; a helmet is advised
A Class 3 chimney that some climbers rate harder, with exposure
Snow and ice that can linger nearly year-round in the upper chutes
Lightning and thunderstorms on the exposed upper mountain
Williamson Bowl is a slow boulder field that sets up a tiring exit at day's end

review.notes: Season Jun-Oct is the window one page gives for the Shepherd Pass trail being snow-free; the summit chutes can hold snow outside it. Anvil Camp distance differs by page (about 7 vs 8 miles); I wrote 7 to 8.

set.overview: White Mountain Peak rises to 14,252 feet in the Inyo National Forest, and its trail is a Class 1 walk along a dirt road with no scrambling. The route heads north past a research station, crosses a high plateau with two dips, then climbs switchbacks on the south side to a small research hut on top. The whole route lies above 11,500 feet, so altitude is the real challenge.
set.approach: From Big Pine, drive east on Highway 168 and north on White Mountain Road, which is paved for 10 miles to Schulman Grove, then about 16 to 17 miles of rough dirt to a locked gate. Plan for a high-clearance vehicle and a full-size spare. No permit or parking fee is required. On foot, follow the road north past the university research station, roughly 2 miles from the gate, then across the plateau and up the switchbacks.
set.descent_text: Return the way you came, along the road. Save some energy for the climbs back out of the two dips on the plateau, and aim to be off the mountain before dark.
hazards: Altitude: the entire route is above 11,500 feet
No water or shade on the route, and strong sun and wind
Summer thunderstorms can build with no shelter on the plateau
Sharp rocks on the access road cause flat tires
Snow can linger on the upper switchbacks into July

review.notes: One guide page carries nearly everything; the Forest Service page confirms a rough dirt road past the research station. 'Inyo National Forest' comes from the Forest Service page. Gain/distance not in fill.

set.overview: Russell's east arete is a Class 3 ridge climb that begins at the saddle with Carillon and runs west over the east summit to the true west summit. The route stays mostly on the right side of the ridge, with sustained exposure and a steep north side, and a few minor technical moves. Many parties camp at Upper Boy Scout Lake and climb it in a day.
hazards: Sustained exposure along the ridge, with a steep north side and some no-fall zones
Loose scree and sand on both the ascent and descent
A misleading cairn can lead onto the north ridge instead of the east ridge
Loose talus and boulder fields on the south-side descent
Snow and ice can cover the ridge later in the year

review.notes: Season skipped: no page names a window (only an access-limit note and mixed-season photos). 'Climb it in a day' is from commenters describing day trips of 9 to 19 hours; the Class 3 rating and the saddle start are from the page.
